title: Nintendo's biggest ROM chip supplier is bowing out of the business
gist: Macronix, Nintendo's main ROM supplier for Switch cartridges, said in its Q3 earnings that ROM production has reached its end as AI-driven demand makes NOR, NAND and eMMC chips more lucrative uses of its capped wafer capacity. Nintendo may face higher cartridge costs from remaining suppliers Rohm and Lapis, partly offset by digital sales already at 61.5% of its business.

themes.theme: AI memory demand crowding out legacy ROM

insights.claim: Macronix said in its third-quarter earnings report that its ROM chip production has reached its end and it will gradually decouple from the game industry.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Exit of a key supplier from a niche chip line shows AI memory economics reshaping fab allocation.

insights.claim: Macronix's ROM production shrank 39% in the last year to just 5% of its business, crowded out by more lucrative NOR, NAND and eMMC memory.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Mix shift toward higher-margin memory is a tailwind for Macronix margins.

insights.claim: With Macronix capacity stuck at 25,000 12-inch wafers a month and $1.2 billion of planned new capacity taking a year or more to come online, low-profit ROM is losing wafer space to higher-earning chips.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Capacity constraints mean memory tightness persists into 2027, sustaining pricing power for memory makers.

insights.claim: AI industry demand for memory and storage has for years pushed up prices and constrained availability of PC components like RAM, SSDs and GPUs, and is now reaching ROM chips for game cartridges.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: AI capex is creating second-order cost inflation in consumer electronics supply chains.

insights.claim: Analyst David Gibson notes Macronix is Nintendo's main memory chip maker for physical Switch and Switch 2 cartridges, leaving Nintendo to rely more on Rohm and Lapis Semiconductor.
insights.speaker: David Gibson
insights.so_what: Supplier concentration shift could raise Nintendo's cartridge COGS and benefit Rohm/Lapis volumes.
insights.locator: That could be an issue for Nintendo

insights.claim: Higher cartridge production costs could flow through to physical game prices; Nintendo already began charging more for some physical games than digital equivalents in 2026.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Price differentials push consumers toward higher-margin digital sales.
insights.locator: That could have a knock-on effect

insights.claim: Nintendo said last month it has no near-term plans to abandon game cartridges, unlike Sony's move away from physical game production.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Nintendo remains exposed to ROM supply costs rather than exiting physical media.

insights.claim: Digital software sales were 61.5% of Nintendo's business in Q2 calendar 2026, up slightly year over year, which over time could offset rising cartridge costs via lower ROM demand.
insights.speaker: David Gibson
insights.so_what: Rising digital mix improves Nintendo margins and cushions the supply hit.
